The term, which may be derived from the name of a Swiss political leader, the Genevan burgomaster Besançon Hugues, was in common use by around 1550. Huguenot was frequently used in reference to those of the Reformed Church of France from the time of the Protestant Reformation. By contrast, the Protestant populations of eastern France, in Alsace, Moselle, and Montbéliard, were mainly Lutherans.

In his Encyclopedia of Protestantism, Hans Hillerbrand wrote that on the eve of the St. Bartholomew's Day massacre in 1572, the Huguenot community made up as much as 10% of the French population. By 1600, it declined to 7–8%, and was reduced further late in the century after the return of persecution under Louis XIV, who instituted the Dragonnades to forcibly convert Protestants, and then finally revoked all Protestant rights in his Edict of Fontainebleau of 1685. In 1686, Protestants comprised just 1% of the population.

The Huguenots were concentrated in the southern and western parts of the Kingdom of France. As Huguenots gained influence and more openly displayed their faith, Catholic hostility grew. A series of religious conflicts followed, known as the French Wars of Religion, fought intermittently from 1562 to 1598. The Huguenots were led by Jeanne d'Albret; her son, the future Henry IV (who would later convert to Catholicism in order to become king); and the princes of Condé. The wars ended with the Edict of Nantes of 1598, which granted the Huguenots substantial religious, political and military autonomy.

Huguenot rebellions in the 1620s resulted in the abolition of their political and military privileges. They retained the religious provisions of the Edict of Nantes until the rule of Louis XIV, who gradually increased persecution of Protestantism until he issued the Edict of Fontainebleau (1685). This ended legal recognition of Protestantism in France and the Huguenots were forced to either convert to Catholicism (possibly as Nicodemites) or flee as refugees; they were subject to violent Dragonnades. Louis XIV claimed the French Huguenot population was reduced from about 900,000 or 800,000 adherents to just 1,000 or 1,500. He exaggerated the decline, but the Dragonnades were devastating for the French Protestant community. The exodus of Huguenots from France created a brain drain, as many of them had occupied important places in society.

The remaining Huguenots faced continued persecution under Louis XV. By the time of his death in 1774, Calvinism had been all but eliminated from France. Persecution of Protestants officially ended with the Edict of Versailles, signed by Louis XVI in 1787. Two years later, with the Revolutionary Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen of 1789, Protestants gained equal rights as citizens.

A term used originally in derision, Huguenot has unclear origins. Various hypotheses have been promoted. The term may have been a combined reference to the Swiss politician Besançon Hugues (died 1532) and the religiously conflicted nature of Swiss republicanism in his time. text:
## Comparison: Huguenots

**Bottom line:** Both sources agree the Huguenots were French Protestants of the Reformed (Calvinist) tradition and that "Huguenot" began as a term of contempt. Beyond that, the two descriptions differ sharply in scope: the Britannica entry in this corpus is a brief OCR fragment that only defines the name and dates its rise to 1560, while the Wikipedia article is a full history covering etymology, demographics, the Wars of Religion, the Edict of Nantes, persecution and revocation under Louis XIV, the refugee exodus, and eventual toleration.

### What Britannica says
Entry E0115, headword "HUGUENOTS" (OCR, scan page 1327):

- "HUGUENOTS, an appellation given by way of contempt to the reformed or Protestant Calvinists of France." (Britannica E0115, scan page 1327)
- "The name had its first rise in 1560; but authors are" — the text cuts off mid-sentence. (Britannica E0115, scan page 1327)

So Britannica identifies the Huguenots as "reformed or Protestant Calvinists of France," gives the term a contemptuous origin, and dates the name's first rise to 1560. That is all this corpus contains for the entry: it is only 156 characters (12 tokens), and the phrases "Edict of Nantes" and "revocation" do not occur in it. The text is noisy OCR and is truncated, so the entry is incomplete here.

### What Wikipedia says
Wikipedia article "Huguenots" (page 75899, revision 1352397655, CC BY-SA 4.0):

- Definition: "The Huguenots ... are a religious group of French Protestants who held to the Reformed (Calvinist) tradition of Protestantism." The term may derive from Genevan burgomaster Besançon Hugues and was in common use by around 1550. (Wikipedia 75899, rev. 1352397655)
- Demographics: up to 10% of the French population on the eve of the 1572 St. Bartholomew's Day massacre; 7–8% by 1600; just 1% by 1686. Eastern France (Alsace, Moselle, Montbéliard) was mainly Lutheran, not Huguenot. (Wikipedia 75899, rev. 1352397655)
- Wars and toleration: French Wars of Religion (1562–1598), led by Jeanne d'Albret, Henry IV, and the princes of Condé; ended by the Edict of Nantes (1598), granting "substantial religious, political and military autonomy." (Wikipedia 75899, rev. 1352397655)
- Persecution and exodus: Huguenot rebellions in the 1620s ended their political/military privileges; Louis XIV's Dragonnades and the Edict of Fontainebleau (1685) revoked Protestant rights, forcing conversion or flight. Louis XIV claimed the community fell from ~800,000–900,000 to 1,000–1,500 (an exaggeration). Refugees fled to the Holy Roman Empire (Brandenburg, Palatinate), Prussia, the Dutch Republic, the Dutch Cape Colony, England, and colonial America (e.g., New York). (Wikipedia 75899, rev. 1352397655; comparison snippets at offsets 13029, 22946, 38985, 45319)
- Later relief: persecution continued under Louis XV; Calvinism was nearly gone by 1774; the Edict of Versailles (1787) ended persecution, and the 1789 Declaration of the Rights of Man gave Protestants equal rights. (Wikipedia 75899, rev. 1352397655)
- Etymology is treated as unclear, with a proposed pun linking Besançon Hugues to Dutch *Huisgenoten* ("housemates") and German *Eidgenosse* ("Confederate"). (Wikipedia 75899, rev. 1352397655)

### Key differences
- **Length/depth:** The matched-pair comparison puts Wikipedia at roughly 500× the length of the Britannica fragment (length ratio 501.5; frequency cosine 0.296; Jaccard 0.047). (challenge_compare, E0115)
- **Coverage:** Britannica (in this corpus) only defines the word and gives an origin date. Wikipedia covers origins, population trends, wars, legal edicts, persecution, refugee destinations, and emancipation.
- **Shared vocabulary:** The overlapping terms are just *huguenots, france, protestant, reformed, name, way, calvinists, given* — i.e., both sources discuss the name and French Protestant identity, but Wikipedia develops the history Britannica omits. (challenge_compare, E0115)

**Caveats:** The Britannica text is OCR from a single scanned page and is truncated mid-sentence, so I cannot confirm whether a fuller Britannica entry exists elsewhere in this corpus. The Wikipedia match is accepted (title similarity 1.0) and describes the same subject.
